title: Eight winds
hook: gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain

segments.voice: Yesterday: drowsy Moggallana and your line, climb the ladder. Did you climb the ladder in the slump? Today, eight things that blow through every life, sleepy or awake. Day six hundred sixty-nine.

People in China tell a story about the poet Su Dongpo. He wrote a poem saying his meditation had grown so steady that the eight winds could not move him, and sent it across the river to his friend, a monk. The monk wrote one rude word on it and sent it back. The poet, furious, rowed straight over to complain. The monk laughed: eight winds can't move you, but one little puff blew you across the river. The story is legend. The eight winds are not. They come from a short sutta in the Book of Eights. Today: eight winds.
screen: `A POET'S PROUD POEM.` → `ONE RUDE WORD BACK.` → `ACROSS THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: In the Book of Eights, the Buddha says: these eight worldly conditions turn the world, and the world turns after them. Gain and loss. Fame and disrepute. Praise and blame. Pleasure and pain. Four pairs. One side of each pair we chase, the other we run from, and between the chasing and the running, a lot of life goes by. In Pali they're the lokadhamma, the ways of the world. The East Asian name, eight winds, is a good picture: they come and go, they push from different sides, and you don't choose the weather. Then, in the next discourse, he makes a sharp point. These eight come to everyone. To the person who hasn't heard the teaching, and to the noble disciple who has. So what's the difference? The untaught person, when gain comes, doesn't reflect: this is impermanent, painful, bound to change. So gain grabs their mind, and when loss comes, loss grabs it too. They're delighted, then crushed, and they don't get free. The taught disciple meets the same eight, and sees them for what they are. Gain doesn't take over the mind. Loss doesn't either. Notice: the disciple still gets praised and still gets blamed. Practice doesn't stop the weather. It changes how much the weather decides. That's the poet's joke, too. He was right about the eight winds, and wrong about himself.
screen: `FOUR PAIRS OF WINDS.` · `THEY COME TO EVERYONE.` · `ONE IS SWEPT AWAY.` · then, large: `ONE SEES THEM PASS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Then ask: which wind blew hardest on me today? A gain or a loss? Some praise, some blame? A pleasure, a pain? Name it, plainly, the way a forecaster names the weather. Feel where it lands in the body. Then just watch it, the way you'd watch wind move a tree. It came. It's moving. It will pass. The tree stays rooted. The bell holds the time.
Eight winds. Gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain: the eight worldly conditions that blow through every life. Today's word.
Your line: let the wind blow past. Today, when praise or blame comes your way, name the wind silently, and let it blow past. Day six hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers in many traditions teach the eight worldly conditions as a check on daily life, and in East Asian Buddhism the 'eight winds' are a common image in sermons and poems about steadiness of mind.

myth: the sutta says awakened disciples stop meeting praise and blame
the eight come to everyone; the difference is whether they take over the mind.
lokadhamma means 'the ways of the world'
the eight worldly conditions that turn the world.
the story of the poet and the monk is told in the sutta
it's a later Chinese story people tell; the eight conditions come from the sutta.

fork.setup: both a taught disciple and an untaught person receive the same praise. what's the difference, in the sutta?
options: the disciple sees it as impermanent, and it doesn't take over the mind.
fork.reveal: the wind blows on both. the disciple sees it as impermanent and bound to change, so praise doesn't seize the mind, and blame doesn't either.

original.note: Pali lokadhamma: 'world-conditions,' the eight worldly conditions.

trapdoor: what you thought: a calm person is someone things don't happen to.
what it means: in AN 8.6 the eight winds blow on everyone; calm is not being carried off by them.
what a scholar hears: 'eight winds' is the East Asian name; the Pali text speaks of worldly conditions that 'turn' the world.
recall: the one who has woken up

sources.ref: The Su Dongpo and Foyin story (Chinese anecdote, Song dynasty)

notes: AN 8.6 paraphrased. Confirm the 'turn the world, and the world turns after them' framing (AN 8.5 Lokadhamma Sutta has it; AN 8.6 has the taught/untaught contrast). The script cites 8.6 per the outline.
The Su Dongpo / Foyin story is presented as legend ('a story people tell'); the 'rude word' is the traditional 'fart' left unspoken. Confirm tone is acceptable.
'Nine hundred years ago' for Su Dongpo (1037–1101) is approximate.

Review (y2 editor pass): the 'turn the world' line is AN 8.5 and the taught/untaught contrast AN 8.6; the teach now says so and AN 8.5 is added to sources. Cut 'nine hundred years ago' (date not in the cited text). Varied the 'Here's the practice' opener.
